Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. In accordance with the latest ICTV taxonomy,
we have revised the manuscript to state that the family Filoviridae comprises nine recognized genera. We
have updated the genus names to Orthoebolavirus and Orthomarburgvirus and now refer to EBOV, SUDV,
BDBV, and RAVV as members of these respective genera throughout the manuscript. We have retained
commonly used species names to ensure clarity for readers.
2. Line 91. The Moderna and Pfizer SARS-CpV-2b mRNA vaccines also express stabilized constructs. It
seems like that should also be mentioned for completeness.
Response: To provide a more complete context, we have included two references highlighting the use of
prefusion-stabilized SARS-CoV-2 spike constructs in mRNA vaccines. Please see page 5, lines 92–94.
3. Line 128 – sentence is not clear.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The sentence has been revised for clarity as follows:
“While the EBOV and SUDV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 trimer and SApNP vaccines elicited serum neutralization
limited to orthoebolaviruses, the RAVV GPΔmuc-P2CT trimer induced detectable cross-genus NAb
responses.” Please see page 6, lines 128-130.
4. Line 335. It might be helpful to define Kifunensine, as an inhibitor of class I α-mannosidases that
prevents α-mannosidases I from trimming mannose residues on glycoproteins, thus resulting in
oligomannose-type glycans.
Response: As the reviewer suggested, we have added a definition of Kifunensine at its first mention in the
text. The revised sentence is as follows: “Supplementing ExpiCHO cultures with kifunensine (Kif) — a
class I α-mannosidase inhibitor that blocks ER glycan processing and leads to accumulation of high
mannose — did not affect neutralizing antibody (NAb) responses.” Please see page 15, lines 337-339.
5. Paragraphs at 441 and 459 – the hypotheses are not clearly stated. I would rewrite these paragraphs
to not be test of hypotheses or explicitly state what the hypotheses are.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have revised the relevant paragraphs to remove
explicit references to a hypothesis and instead directly describe the experiments and the immunological
3
parameters being investigated. These changes clarify the intent of the experiments without framing them as
formal hypothesis tests. Please see page 20, lines 436–438, as well as paragraphs on pages 21-23.
6. Line 758 – would rewrite this to say that future studies are needed to determine whether improved in
vitro antigenicity correlate with improved in vivo immunogenicity as well as protection from disease.
Might be better to move this sentence down to the paragraph at line 784.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. As recommended, we removed the original
sentence from line 758 and incorporated a revised version into the paragraph into the future directions
section. After outlining the first objective on antibody epitope mapping for wildtype and glycan-modified
GP vaccine constructs, we added the following sentence: “Such analyses may explain why improved
epitope exposure following glycan trimming did not translate into stronger NAb responses in vivo” This
revision more clearly underscores the need for future studies to determine whether enhanced in vitro
antigenicity correlates with in vivo immunogenicity and protection. Please see page 37, lines 821–822.
7. Line 778. The term “Kif-treated, oligomannose-rich immunogens” doesn’t seem accurate [I get the
jargon]. The cells used to produce the immunogen were Kif-treated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We revised this sentence and now it reads: while
oligomannose-rich immunogens – produced in the presence of kifunensine (Kif) – induced the strongest
bAb and NAb responses at most timepoints.” Please see page 36, lines 811-812.
8. Line 782 – Consider another word besides “discrepancy.” I would mention these results in the abstract.
It’s important to point out that” there may not be a general glycan strategy that fits all viral GP vaccines.”
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have replaced the word “discrepancy” with
“differences” and revise the sentence (see page 36, lines 814-816). While we agree with the reviewer that
this finding is important, we are unable to include it in the Abstract due to strict 200-word limit. To
emphasize its significance, we have added a sentence to the final paragraph of the Introduction: “Although
no universal glycan modification strategy may apply to all viral GPs, enriching the filovirus GP glycan
shield with oligomannose-type glycans improved vaccine-induced NAb responses in mice.” (see pages 6-
7, lines 131-133).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents a promising strategy for developing next-generation filovirus vaccines by
stabilizing GP glycoprotein structures, optimizing their display on self-assembling nanoparticles, and
exploring the effects of glycan modifications. The study includes high-resolution structural analyses of GPs
from multiple filoviruses, though these structural data are not fully integrated into the immunogen design
process. In addition, the authors investigate and compare the lymph node dynamics of GP antigens in a
mouse model, providing insights into how antigen presentation differs between soluble and nanoparticle-
displayed formats. This multi-faceted approach offers valuable data for vaccine development. However,
several aspects require clarification or further validation, particularly regarding the rationale connecting
structural and immunological components, methodological choices in antigenicity assessment, and the
interpretation of immunization results. The manuscript would benefit from clearer explanations, stronger
statistical support, and more direct evidence to support some of the conclusions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful evaluation and for recognizing the potential of our
multi-faceted approach to inform next-generation filovirus vaccine development. We also acknowledge the
constructive concerns regarding the integration of structural data into immunogen design, interpretation of
immune responses, and presentation of supporting data. In response, we have clarified the rationale linking
our structural findings to vaccine design, expanded methodological explanations, and strengthened the
interpretation of key immunological findings. We hope that these revisions address the reviewer’s concerns
and help to more clearly convey the rigor of our work. Based on the reviewers’ comments, we have included
4
new data from immunohistological analysis and mouse immunization. We have also made edits throughout
the manuscript to improve clarity and flow. All changes are highlighted in the revised manuscript.
Major concerns:
1. The manuscript asserts that structural data supported immunogen design, but it does not
convincingly establish this connection. If the structures did not directly inform the design of vaccine
constructs, then separating the structural and vaccine design components into two focused
manuscripts should be considered. This would help sharpen the manuscript’s message and clarify
the individual contributions of each part.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. Our structural analyses, combined with in
vitro characterization, form the foundation of our immunogen design strategy. The structural data confirmed
that the stabilizing mutations preserved the native-like prefusion conformation of GP and maintained key
neutralizing epitopes, which is an essential validation step prior to nanoparticle display and immunological
evaluation. In our previous study [He et al., Nat. Commun. 12, 2633 (2021)], we introduced mutations in
the HR1c bend and HR2 stalk of EBOV GP, yielding two lead designs: GPΔmuc-WL2P2 and GPΔmuc-
WL2P4. While both GP constructs were functional, WL2P2 exhibited a biphasic thermal denaturation profile
indicative of structural heterogeneity, while WL2P4 showed a more favorable, single-peak DSC profile. In
this study, we extended both designs to SUDV and BDBV and found that WL2P4 consistently showed
superior biochemical and biophysical properties across all three orthoebolavirus backbones. To validate the
structural fidelity of this design, we determined the crystal structure of EBOV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 and
compared it with previously solved WL2 and WL2P2 structures, establishing a clear structural rationale for
selecting WL2P4 as the optimal platform. We further determined the cryo-EM structure of SUDV GPΔmuc-
WL2P4 in complex with CA45, confirming the structural integrity of WL2P4 in a different orthoebolavirus
backbone and resolving local epitope features at a conserved bNAb site. In summary, the crystallographic
and cryo-EM data were critical for demonstrating that our rationally designed immunogens adopt native-
like conformations and preserve key neutralizing epitopes. Presenting the structural and immunogen design
components together reflects the iterative nature of the approach and underscores the rationale linking
structural validation to downstream immunogenicity. We believe a unified presentation most effectively
conveys the significance and translational potential of our findings.
2. Although the study provides data on antigen retention and germinal center responses, the
comparison of functional antibody responses—particularly neutralizing and cross-neutralizing
antibody titers—between different vaccine constructs is not clearly presented or discussed.
This
makes it difficult to determine whether nanoparticle display confers an actual benefit in protective
immune responses beyond improved antigen presentation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. In this study, we examined lymph node trafficking
and immune responses elicited by SUDV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 in both trimeric and SApNP formats. Compared
to soluble trimers, SApNPs exhibited prolonged retention in lymph node follicles, greater association with
follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), and more robust and sustained germinal center (GC) reactions. To assess
vaccine-induced functional antibody responses, we measured both binding antibody (bAb) and neutralizing
antibody (NAb) titers. E2p and I3-01v9b SApNPs consistently elicited higher EC titers at all time points
50
compared to the trimer. For NAb responses, both SApNPs also produced the highest ID titers after two
50
doses, although the differences from the trimer group were not statistically significant. These data suggest
that nanoparticle display may accelerate the development of functional antibody responses, consistent with
enhanced antigen delivery and GC activation. We note that the current immunization schedule was designed
to provide an initial readout of immunogenicity rather than optimize the response. It is possible that the full
benefit of SApNPs will become more apparent with extended dosing intervals, which will be explored in
future studies. Additional discussion can be found in our response to Comment #3.
3. Relatedly, while the nanoparticle-based vaccines elicit stronger markers of immune activation,
such as germinal center formation and lymph node retention, this enhancement does not appear to
5
translate into consistently stronger neutralization. This disconnect should be explicitly addressed
in the discussion, as it raises questions about the practical advantage of nanoparticle presentation
in the absence of clear improvements in functional antibody responses.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As detailed in the manuscript, multivalent
display of GPΔmuc trimers on SApNPs enhances antigen retention in lymph node follicles, increases
association with follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), and promotes more robust and durable germinal center
(GC) reactions compared to soluble trimers. After two doses, SApNPs elicited the highest EC and ID
50 50
titers, consistent with the stronger GC responses observed in the lymph node analysis. However, following
additional immunizations, the soluble trimers generated NAb titers comparable to those of the SApNPs,
likely reflecting a plateau in the SApNP-induced responses by week 8. These findings suggest that while
SApNPs accelerate the development of functional antibody responses, repeated dosing can enable soluble
trimers to achieve similar outcomes. Thus, a key advantage of nanoparticle vaccines lies in their ability to
induce potent responses with fewer doses. As noted in our response to Comment #2, the current regimen
was designed to obtain an initial immunogenicity readout rather than optimized for maximal response, and
extended dosing intervals may further enhance the immunogenicity of SApNPs. Lastly, to support broader
applicability, we included results from male mouse immunizations alongside previously reported female
cohorts (see pages 31-32, lines 705–717).
Minor concerns:
1. The cryo-EM report appears technically sound, but the structure validation would benefit from the
inclusion of correlation coefficients and EMRinger scores in the refinement statistics. These are
widely used metrics that improve the transparency and reliability of structural assessments and
would strengthen the claims about model quality.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. As recommended, we performed EMRinger
validation for the cryo-EM structure, which yielded a score of 2.60. This value is consistent with good side-
chain placement and overall model quality. We have included this information in the revised manuscript
(see page 11, lines 242).
2. The redesign of the I3-01v9a nanoparticle to optimize its N-terminal geometry for GP stalk
compatibility is a notable feature, but the manuscript does not present comparative data to
demonstrate the necessity or functional benefit of this modification. Including a comparison of
structural or biochemical outcomes before and after the redesign would better support the rationale
for this engineering effort.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. In our previous study [He et al., Nat. Commun. 12,
2633 (2021)], we reported I3-01v9 SApNPs displaying EBOV GPΔmuc-WL2P2 trimers, in which a 10GS
linker was used to anchor the GPΔmuc trimer to the wider N-termini of the I3-01v9 subunits arranged
around each threefold axis of the particle surface. The SEC profile of these non-optimized I3-01v9 SApNPs
(Fig. 4f in that publication), obtained using a Superose 6 Increase column, showed a noticeable peak
corresponding to unassembled species. In the current study, the SEC profile of EBOV GPΔmuc-presenting
I3-01v9b SApNPs, with optimized N-terminal geometry and no flexible linker between the GP and NP
scaffold, exhibited a reduced trimer peak and higher NP yield compared to the earlier I3-01v9 construct
(Fig. 3d, left). Moreover, when I3-01v9b was used to present SUDV and BDBV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 trimers,
we observed comparable or improved SEC profiles, with negligible amounts of unassembled trimer species
(Fig. 3d, middle and right). Together, these results demonstrate that the computationally redesigned I3-
01v9b significantly improves both the biochemical properties and assembly efficiency of the GPΔmuc-
presenting SApNPs. We have revised the manuscript to clarify the rationale for this redesign in the Results
(page 13, lines 275-281) and further context in the Discussion section (pages 34-35, lines 770-792) to
emphasize its broader utility as an NP carrier for diverse viral GPs containing a narrow stalk.
6
3. Several RMSD-based structural comparisons presented in the results rely on a limited subset of
atoms, which may not reflect the full extent of structural similarity or divergence. Broader atom
selections, such as inclusion of entire domains or full protomers, would yield more robust
comparisons and improve the reliability of the conclusions drawn from these analyses.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We would like to clarify that all resolved
backbone Cα atoms in the GPΔmuc protomer—the broader atom selection referenced by the reviewer—
were included in the comparison between the crystal structures of EBOV GPΔmuc-WL2P2 and -WL2P4.
In
addition, a focused comparison of the HR1c bend was performed to assess local conformational differences
in this critical region for GP stabilization (see pages 10-11, lines 224–227). For the cryo-EM structure of
SUDV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 in complex with CA45 Fab, the map resolution (3.1–3.4 Å) limited confident
backbone modeling in certain regions (see our response to reviewer #1, question 1, and Fig. S2f). As a
result, the number of Cα atoms included in RMSD-based calculations for the cryo-EM model was smaller
than for the crystal structures (154 vs. 243 atoms). Moreover, due to <80% sequence identity among EBOV,
SUDV, and BDBV GPs, some residues were excluded due to alignment gaps or divergence in non-
conserved structural regions. The structural comparisons presented in the manuscript were carefully
designed to maximize the inclusion of well-resolved, structurally aligned backbone atoms while avoiding
potential artifacts from poorly modeled or non-homologous regions. We believe this approach provides a
robust and interpretable evaluation of structural similarity and divergence across the filovirus GPs analyzed.
4. The rationale behind the use of different immunization intervals for the initial versus glycan-
modified groups is not explained. This difference in scheduling could influence immune outcomes
and complicates interpretation of comparative results, so it is important that the authors clarify
their reasoning and address how this may affect their conclusions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. The mouse immunization data shown in Figs. 9 and
10 were generated from two separate studies conducted at different stages of our research, each with its
own experimental rationale and design. In our first study, we aimed to assess antibody responses induced
by rationally designed filovirus constructs. The decision to use longer intervals was based on our lymph
node analysis, which demonstrated that GPmuc-presenting SApNPs are retained in lymph node follicles
for over eight weeks (Fig. 6) and elicit robust, long-lived GC reactions at weeks 5 and 8 after a single-dose
injection (Fig. 8). Based on these findings, we adopted an immunization schedule with 6-week intervals
between the second and third, and third and fourth doses. NAb responses were detectable at weeks 5, 11,
and 17, and plateaued by week 11 after three doses. These results suggested that extended intervals and
more than three doses may not be necessary to achieve a potent NAb response. Around the same time, we
conducted a separate study on RSV F trimer vaccines, recently reported in Nature Communications [Lee et
al., Nat. Commun. 15, 9939 (2024)]. In that study, we found that a shorter interval was sufficient to elicit
strong NAb responses. Based on these insights, our second filovirus vaccine study, which was focused on
glycan-modified constructs, used a shorter 3-week interval between doses. This shorter regimen is also
consistent with our standard “screening” approach in other proof-of-concept vaccine studies.
We agree that the two studies do not represent a direct head-to-head comparison of wildtype versus glycan
modified antigens. However, both studies used the same 3-week interval between the first and second doses,
allowing for a direct comparison of early-stage NAb responses. In the submitted manuscript, statistical
analyses were performed only for serum samples collected at week 5 (following the second dose), based on
ID values. For samples collected after the third immunization, ID titers were plotted but not subjected
50 50
to statistical analysis due to differences in immunization schedules. To clarify this limitation, we included
the following statement in the last paragraph of the Results section: “However, due to differences in
immunization protocols (e.g., dosing intervals), additional in vivo studies are needed to confirm these
results.” (see page 32, lines 720–722).
5. The use of IgG-format antibodies in BLI assays to assess GP antigenicity is not ideal due to avidity
effects, which obscure true affinity differences and reduce the assay’s sensitivity to detect variation
7
between constructs. The use of Fab fragments would provide a more accurate 1:1 binding model
and allow for a clearer comparison of antigen binding properties between trimeric and
nanoparticle-displayed immunogens.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. In general, we agree that Fabs offer a more
accurate 1:1 binding model in BLI assays, particularly for monomeric or single-epitope antigens. However,
this approach faces challenges when applied to GPΔmuc trimers, which display three identical binding sites
per trimer, and even greater challenges when these trimers are multivalently displayed on SApNPs.
An additional constraint arises from the biosensor configuration itself. The commonly used anti-human Fc
Capture (AHC) biosensor is not suitable for large particles with dense surface antigen display. During the
early development of our BLI assays in 2017, we collaborated with FortéBio’s R&D scientists to evaluate
a panel of biosensors on various SApNPs (24-mer FR vs. 60-mer E2p/I3-01). These studies showed that
anti-human IgG Quantitation (AHQ) biosensors offered the most reliable and reproducible signals for large,
virus-sized particles. In contrast, AHC biosensors often yielded artificially low or negative signals, likely
due to steric hindrance or signal dampening caused by densely packed surface antigens. AHQ biosensors
are designed to quantify analyte density in solution and are therefore better suited for detecting antigens
presented on large protein NPs. While this setup does incorporate avidity effects, particularly with IgGs,
it
remains the only configuration that produces measurable BLI responses for both trimers and SApNPs.
To further evaluate the reviewer’s suggestion and demonstrate the limitations of Fab-based assays, we
produced CA45 and ADI-15878 Fabs and performed BLI assays using FAB2G biosensors. These assays
yielded consistent profiles for EBOV and SUDV GPΔmuc-WL2P4 trimers. However, the corresponding
SApNPs generated minimal or undetectable signals using FAB2G biosensors, similar to what we observed
with AHC biosensors. These findings reinforce our conclusion that using IgGs paired with AHQ sensors
provides the most practical and interpretable method for antigenic comparison between trimers and SApNPs.
For these reasons, we continue to use IgGs with AHQ biosensors in the BLI assays presented in this study.
8
6. The data on RAVV GP trimer immunization lack statistical support for the claim that the wildtype
trimer is more effective than the glycan-trimmed versions. Additionally, the conclusion that RAVV
GP is “more immunogenic” or holds promise as a pan-filovirus immunogen is currently
speculative and should be supported with comparative data or a more cautious interpretation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We agree that the current data do not support
a statistically robust comparison between wildtype and glycan-trimmed RAVV GPΔmuc trimers, as the
two groups were immunized using different schedules (week 17 vs. week 11). As such, these neutralization
data are presented as observational rather than comparative. Nonetheless, the similar trends observed for
EBOV and SUDV GPΔmuc immunogens, with and without glycan trimming, provide contextual support
for the RAVV findings. To assess the NAb responses elicited by RAVV GPΔmuc trimers, we purified total
IgG from mouse sera to eliminate nonspecific background in pseudovirus assays. Control experiments using
LCMV pseudoparticles confirmed that the purified IgG did not exhibit nonspecific neutralization. We then
tested these IgG samples against EBOV-Makona, SUDV-Gulu, and BDBV-Uganda pseudoviruses. Both
wildtype and glycan-trimmed RAVV GPΔmuc trimers elicited detectable cross-neutralizing activity against
the tested orthoebolaviruses. This finding suggests that RAVV GP may possess intrinsic immunogenic
potential. However, we agree that the current mouse data are limited in scope and do not support a definitive
conclusion. We have revised the manuscript accordingly to present these findings more cautiously and to
highlight the need for additional in vivo studies evaluating the inclusion of RAVV GP as a component of a
pan-filovirus vaccine. Please see pages 28 and 31, as well as page 32, lines 724-725, in the Results section,
and page 37, lines 827-830, in the Discussion section.
9

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have carefully addressed each of my concerns. I have nmo further comments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have made substantial improvements, and the manuscript is much clearer and more cohesive. Several earlier concerns have been addressed with helpful additions, while a few areas could still benefit from further clarification or discussion.
Major:
1. The authors’ explanation connecting structural validation to the selection of WL2P4 is convincing.
2. No revision was provided. The lack of statistical significance in neutralizing antibody responses between different vaccine constructs needs to be clearly described and discussed.
3. Adding data from male cohorts is a welcome expansion. The “accelerated kinetics” interpretation is now better framed, though still based on non-harmonized datasets. Quantitative metrics such as area-under-the-curve or time-to-threshold analyses could provide a more robust basis for this point.
Minor:
1. The inclusion of the EMRinger score is appreciated. However, the model–map correlation coefficients was not provided as suggested.
2. I3-01v9b redesign comment was well addressed.
3. The explanation for atom selection is reasonable, and the current analyses are acceptable.
4. The explanation for the differing schedules is now clear and limitations are acknowledged. To avoid potential misinterpretation, visual contrasts between non-equivalent regimens might be better placed in the Supplement.
5. The additional experiments with Fabs help to illustrate the technical challenges, and it would be helpful to include these results, even if limited, in the Supplement. Stating explicitly that the reported IgG/AHQ values represent apparent rather than intrinsic affinities would make the interpretation more transparent.
6. The moderated language on the RAVV GP immunogenicity and contextualization of the findings make this section appropriate.
Additional comments regarding the cryo-EM structure:
Specifically, the Ramachandran favored score is 92.79%, which is slightly low for a 3.1 Å structure, and there are CaBLAM outliers at 5.38%, indicating backbone geometry concerns. The correlation coefficients are mixed: CC(mask) = 0.73 and CC(volume) = 0.72 are reasonable, but CC(box) = 0.60, CC(peaks) = 0.51, and CC(ligand) = 0.53 are noticeably low. These values suggest suboptimal model-to-map fit, with evidence of overbuilding and unexplained map density in certain regions.
From a biological perspective, this structure is central to validating the authors’ rational antigen design strategy, demonstrating that the engineered GP can present a native-like conformation. The antibody epitope region appears relatively well-resolved and interpretable, which is essential for supporting their mechanistic conclusions. However, other regions of the GP trimer are less well-resolved, reducing overall confidence in the global model.
If the authors are unable to further refine and improve the map and model, I strongly recommend that they report the limitations transparently. This should include a clear statement in the text, as well as complete validation data as mentioned above, with local resolution maps, and representative density figures for different regions. Clear reporting will allow readers to appropriately interpret and utilize the structure.

No further comments
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):

and more cohesive. Several earlier concerns have been addressed with helpful additions, while a few areas
could still benefit from further clarification or discussion.
Response: We thank Reviewer #3 for the thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our manuscript. This
is the second round of revision, and we are pleased that most of the reviewer’s earlier concerns have been
addressed. The other two reviewers have expressed satisfaction with the revised manuscript, and we have
carefully considered the additional points raised here. We are grateful for these insightful comments, which
have helped us further refine the text and clarify key aspects of the study. We have also made focused edits
to improve clarity and flow, all of which are highlighted in the revised version.
1. No revision was provided. The lack of statistical significance in neutralizing antibody responses
between different vaccine constructs needs to be clearly described and discussed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. In the first mouse study (Fig. 9), we assessed antibody
responses to rationally designed filovirus GPmuc vaccine constructs in trimer and SApNP (E2p and I3-
01v9b) forms, whereas in the second mouse study (Fig. 10), we focused on different glycan modifications
of the same constructs. We agree with the reviewer that the NAb responses (ID titers) did not show
50
significant differences between trimers and SApNPs (Fig. 9), although Kif-treated groups reached statistical
significance in several cases (Fig. 10).
Several factors may explain the lack of statistical significance between vaccine constructs. First, epitope
exposure differs between soluble trimers (fully exposed) and NP-displayed forms, where IFL and stalk
epitopes are less accessible. As a result, the proportion of functional NAbs targeting specific epitopes likely
differs. Increasing NP size and tuning antigen spacing may improve epitope exposure and enhance NAb
responses (Nguyen et al., NPJ Vaccines 2021, 6:70; Ellis et al., Cell Rep. 2023, 42:113552). Indeed, we are
actively optimizing the SApNP platform to generate size-adjustable NPs. Second, longitudinal analysis
showed that NAb responses (ID titers) tracked well with binding antibody (bAb) responses measured by
50 50
ID titers were more variable. Similar differences between trimer and NP immunogens have been reported
50
for EBOV GP (Powell et al., Front. Immunol. 2022, 13:942897; Xu et al, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.
2024, 121:e2316960121), likely depending on construct design and immunization regimen. Finally, animal
models may contribute to the weaker significance in NAb responses. Mice are known to produce antibodies
with shorter HCDR3 loops, which limit access to IFL and stalk epitopes on NPs. These epitopes may be
more effectively targeted in rabbits, non-human primates, or humans.
Based on the reviewer’s suggestion, we modified the Results for Fig. 9 (page 27, lines 598-599; page 28,
line 625) to clearly state the lack of statistical significance with a brief explanation (page 29, lines 645-651).
We also modified the Discussion to address possible causes and solutions (page 37, lines 837-843).
1
2. Adding data from male cohorts is a welcome expansion. The “accelerated kinetics” interpretation
is now better framed, though still based on non-harmonized datasets. Quantitative metrics such as
area-under-the-curve or time-to-threshold analyses could provide a more robust basis for this point.
Response: We thank the reviewer for recognizing the inclusion of new experimental data from a mouse
immunization study addressing sex as a biological variable. In response to this comment, we added a section
in the Discussion describing the possible accelerated development of functional antibody responses induced
by SApNP display (page 37, lines 823-829). Because vaccine injections and endpoint serum collections
were performed at different time points, area under the curve (AUC) and time-to-threshold (TTT) analyses
could not be applied consistently across all conditions. To avoid potential misinterpretation, additional in
vivo experiments will be required to verify this conclusion. We have revised the manuscript accordingly to
highlight the need for further in vivo investigation (page 33, lines 735-738).
3. The inclusion of the EMRinger score is appreciated. However, the model–map correlation
coefficients was not provided as suggested.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have included map–model correlation coefficients
and other key validation parameters for our cryo-EM structure, along with 27 reported orthoebolavirus GP–
antibody complexes from the EMDB, in Fig. S2f. The Results section was revised to reference these data
and to note the less optimal coefficients (page 11, lines 241-243).
4. The explanation for the differing schedules is now clear and limitations are acknowledged. To
avoid potential misinterpretation, visual contrasts between non-equivalent regimens might be
better placed in the Supplement.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. Based on the first mouse study of antibody responses

50
groups plateaued after three doses. Therefore, in our second study, we calculated and plotted longitudinal
EC and ID titers on one graph to provide a more complete view of the datasets (Fig. 10). As expected,
50 50
most peak titers were observed after three immunizations, either at week 11 or week 8. To avoid potential
misinterpretation, we have clarified this point in the revised manuscript (page 33, lines 735-738) and added
a statement in the Fig. 10 legend (page 77, lines 1932-1935).
5. The additional experiments with Fabs help to illustrate the technical challenges, and it would be
helpful to include these results, even if limited, in the Supplement. Stating explicitly that the
reported IgG/AHQ values represent apparent rather than intrinsic affinities would make the
interpretation more transparent.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have included additional BLI data on Fabs in the
Supplementary Materials (Fig. S3l) and reported it in the Results section (pages 15-16, lines 336-341). We
also clarified that the reported IgG/AHQ values represent apparent rather than intrinsic affinities.

perspective, this structure is central to validating the authors’ rational antigen design strategy,
demonstrating that the engineered GP can present a native-like conformation. The antibody epitope
region appears relatively well-resolved and interpretable, which is essential for supporting their
mechanistic conclusions. However, other regions of the GP trimer are less well-resolved, reducing
overall confidence in the global model. If the authors are unable to further refine and improve the
map and model, I strongly recommend that they report the limitations transparently. This should
include a clear statement in the text, as well as complete validation data as mentioned above, with
2
local resolution maps, and representative density figures for different regions. Clear reporting will
allow readers to appropriately interpret and utilize the structure.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The Ramachandran favored percentage
(92.79%) is slightly below the ideal (>95%), but with 0% in the disallowed region, the overall model
remains within acceptable standards. We also acknowledge that CC(box), CC(peaks), and CC(ligand) are
toward the lower end and may reflect suboptimal map-model fit. The lower CC(box) likely reflects missing
flexible regions in the density map, particularly the CA45 constant domains (heavy: S113-T211; light:
T109-S215), the GP glycan cap, and the C-terminal GP2 stalk (C601-E611). The reduced CC(peaks) is
attributable to weak side-chain density, while the lower CC(ligand) values reflect the intrinsic flexibility of
glycans, which are generally poorly resolved in cryo-EM maps. Importantly, the GP-CA45 interface was
well resolved and interpretable, providing key evidence for our rational design of GP presenting native-
like bNAb epitopes. Thus, excluding less resolved regions does not compromise the structural quality or
biological interpretation of the antigen–antibody interface.
To further address the reviewer’s concern about model quality, we surveyed 27 cryo-EM structures of
orthoebolavirus GP-antibody complexes in the EMDB and compared map-model correlation coefficients
and other key parameters with those of our structure. Our values fall within the reported range, though some
are toward the lower end. In the GP trimer, three regions—GP1 (A187–L218), GP2 (E522–N525), and the
C-terminal stalk (P612–N637)—were excluded from the final model due to limited local resolution. The
CA45 constant domains were also excluded because their density was poorly resolved owing to intrinsic
flexibility. Similar exclusions or partial modeling of these regions are common among reported GP–NAb
structures in the EMDB, suggesting that their absence does not compromise biological interpretation.
Finally, we agree that the limitations of our cryo-EM analysis should be reported with transparency. We
have added a model validation plot and summary to the Supplemental Information (Fig. S2f), revised the
Results section to describe the suboptimal map–model fit (pages 11, lines 241–243; pages 11–12, lines
247–250), and included a statement in the Discussion (page 35, lines 777–779) to highlight these limitations
and reference the detailed model evaluation (Fig. S2f).
3
